name: NeuralPath ChromaLift Spectral Vision Mod
body_location: retinal (bilateral photoreceptor surface coating with optic nerve signal bridge)
description:
ChromaLift applies a molecularly thin photoactive lattice to the retinal surface of both eyes via a non-surgical ophthalmic instillation process — essentially eye drops administered in a clinical setting, with the lattice self-assembling over the photoreceptor layer within 72 hours. The lattice introduces supplementary cone-analog receptors sensitive to near-ultraviolet (350-380nm) and near-infrared (700-780nm) wavelengths beyond standard human visual range, and a signal bridge node behind the eye translates the novel wavelength data into a cortical color language the brain learns to interpret as new distinct colors. The result is not a dramatic tactical overlay but a quiet expansion of the visible palette: certain flowers glow with patterns invisible to unmodified eyes, the heat-shimmer above a coffee cup takes on a faint amber hue, fabrics and dyes that appear identical in standard light reveal distinct undertones. The brain's adaptation period, during which it learns to interpret the new input, typically takes three to six weeks.

ChromaLift users frequently describe the adaptation period as one of the most disorienting and beautiful experiences of their lives — the world they've always known slowly reveals a layer they never knew was missing. Visual artists, textile designers, tattoo artists, and anyone working in color-sensitive fields get it for professional reasons. But a substantial portion of ChromaLift installs are purely experiential — people who simply want to see more of the world. It has developed a particular following in GLMZ's urban art communities, where ChromaLift-specific murals and installations exist that are invisible or incomplete to unmodified viewers. The implant requires no ongoing power beyond what the body provides, has no moving parts, and short of direct ocular trauma, lasts indefinitely — which makes the one-time price feel reasonable to the many people who spend years saving for it.
installation_requirements: Licensed ophthalmic clinic only; self-assembling lattice instillation (eye drops) followed by 72-hour light-restriction recovery; no surgical incision required but clinical monitoring mandatory
maintenance: Annual ophthalmic check to verify lattice integrity; signal bridge node firmware update via external NFC wand at clinic; no battery replacement required; lattice is permanent unless chemically dissolved

side_effects: Disorientation and visual 'noise' during the 3-6 week adaptation period as the brain learns new color channels
Photosensitivity to certain UV light sources (tanning equipment, some industrial lighting) — standard ChromaLift post-care includes UV-filter eyewear for the first month
Vivid and unusually colorful dreams throughout the adaptation period, sometimes persisting long-term
Rare cases of mild synesthetic bleed — small percentage of users begin associating the new color channels with sounds or emotions, which most describe as pleasant but occasionally overwhelming
cultural_context: ChromaLift carries a quiet prestige that other sensory implants don't quite match — there is something about expanded color perception that touches on the philosophical, on what it means to experience beauty, that elevates it above the purely utilitarian. In art communities across Tiers 2 through 4, it's a marker of serious engagement with the visual world. The ChromaLift art underground in GLMZ is substantial: galleries that require the implant for full appreciation, street murals with UV layers, textile pieces that only resolve into their complete pattern under expanded vision. This has created some tension — accusations of exclusivity, of art becoming gated behind a purchase. Counter-artists deliberately work only in standard-spectrum to push back. In professional contexts, the implant is essentially expected in high-end design, fashion, and certain medical imaging fields. In Tier 1, it's aspirational — a thing people save for over years, a luxury that nonetheless feels more like a right than an indulgence.
known_users: Visual artists, painters, muralists, and installation artists
Textile designers, dye workers, and fashion industry professionals
Medical imaging technicians and dermatology specialists
People pursuing purely experiential aesthetic enhancement
story_hooks: A ChromaLift user contacts the crew after she notices that a particular building in the Gray Zone — one that looks like an abandoned warehouse to standard vision — has an elaborate UV-spectrum marking system on its exterior that only ChromaLift users can see, and she's been following the pattern for weeks.

A recent batch of ChromaLift instillations from a specific clinic has produced an unusual adaptation effect: users are all perceiving the same new color where there should be individual variation, and when they compare descriptions, they realize they're all seeing it in the same location — a specific address in Tier 4.

The crew needs to authenticate a piece of evidence — a document whose validity marking is encoded in a UV-spectrum dye pattern. None of them have ChromaLift, and the only person in their network who does has just gone missing.
